title: Death Count In Nepal's Himlung Himal Peak Avalanche Reaches 15 - NDTV
description: Death Count In Nepal's Himlung Himal Peak Avalanche Reaches 15  NDTV
publisher.title: NDTV
full_article:
Kathmandu: Eight more bodies of those killed in an avalanche on Nepal's Himlung Himal peak were recovered on Thursday, taking the death count to 15, while one person remains missing.

The avalanche struck the base camp of the 7,126-metre Himlung Himal peak in the Nar Phu area of Nepal's Manang district, burying tents where 16 people, including support staff and mountain guides, were taking shelter.

President of the Nepal National Mountain Guides Association said eight bodies were recovered from the mountain on Thursday.

Two bodies each were recovered from the mountain on Sunday and Monday, while three were recovered on Wednesday.

A 14-member rescue team was deployed to search for the missing workers and guides, who usually provide logistical and other support to climbing expeditions.

Around two dozen Nepali high-altitude workers and guides from Himalayan Holidays and Imagine Nepal Trek and Expedition had travelled from Kathmandu to Himlung Himal about two weeks ago to prepare for the climbing season.

title: Jersey City Designates September as Nepal Heritage Month, Honoring Nepali Community’s Contributions - nepyork
description: Jersey City Designates September as Nepal Heritage Month, Honoring Nepali Community’s Contributions  nepyork
publisher.title: nepyork
full_article:
JERSEY CITY, N.J. — The Jersey City Municipal Council has designated September as Nepal Heritage Month, recognizing the history, culture and contributions of the city’s growing Nepali community.

The council approved the designation as Resolution 26-584 during its regular meeting on Sept. 23. The measure was listed as agenda item 10.5.

The resolution describes Jersey City as one of the most ethnically, culturally, linguistically and internationally diverse cities in the United States, noting that immigrant and diaspora communities contribute to the city’s social and economic life through cultural preservation, entrepreneurship, civic engagement and public service.

The resolution recognizes Nepali Americans and Nepali-speaking residents as an important part of Jersey City’s multicultural community. It highlights their contributions in areas including business, professional services, education, health care, social services, arts and culture, community leadership, volunteerism and advocacy.

It also recognizes the community’s efforts to preserve and share Nepal’s languages, music, dance, cuisine, traditional attire, festivals, spiritual traditions and cultural values.

September, the resolution notes, carries particular historical and cultural significance for Nepal and the global Nepali diaspora. It references Nepal’s Constitution Day, or Samvidhan Diwas, observed on Sept. 20 to commemorate the promulgation of the country’s constitution in 2015.

The resolution also notes that Jersey City formally recognized the Nepali festivals of Dashain and Tihar through an official city proclamation on Oct. 1, 2025. It additionally recognized Dr. Bishnu Maya Pariyar, a member of the Jersey City Women’s Advisory Board, for her community leadership and efforts to strengthen ties between the city and its Nepali residents.

The Jersey City Municipal Council’s resolution designating September as Nepal Heritage Month recognizes the contributions of Nepali Americans to the city’s cultural and civic life. Photo courtesy of Dr. Bishnu Maya Pariyar.

“Establishing Nepal Heritage Month will provide an annual opportunity to recognize the history, culture, traditions, achievements, resilience and contributions of Nepali people,” the resolution states.

The designation encourages schools, community organizations, cultural institutions, businesses, public agencies and residents to participate in educational, artistic, cultural and civic programs celebrating Nepal and Nepali American heritage.

The resolution was attested by City Clerk Sean J. Gallagher and signed by Council President Denise Ridley, Councilman-at-Large Rolando R. Lavarro, and Councilman Tom Zuppa of Ward C.

title: A new chapter for the Nepali Congress: Reflections at a moment of transition - english.onlinekhabar.com
description: A new chapter for the Nepali Congress: Reflections at a moment of transition  english.onlinekhabar.com
publisher.title: english.onlinekhabar.com
full_article:
As the Nepali Congress, having remained at the centre of Nepal’s modern political history for eight decades, moves toward its 15th general convention, the present moment invites both remembrance and reflection. It also offers an opportunity to ask what the democratic tradition represented by the Nepali Congress has meant to Nepal, how the country it helped shape has changed, where the party stands today, and what that tradition will need in order to remain relevant.

No political tradition in Nepal has been more closely associated with the country’s struggle for democracy, the expansion of political participation and the making of its modern political institutions than the one the Nepali Congress represents, and the Congress led that struggle at each stage, setting its democratic demands, sustaining its movements and giving its gains institutional form. Its significance extends beyond the history of an organisation: it forms part of the larger story of how Nepal came to understand citizenship, representation, constitutional government and the possibilities of democratic politics.

That history belongs to a period in which Nepal moved from a highly restricted political order toward a more open and representative one, and political participation gradually acquired a wider meaning. The Nepali Congress was the principal torchbearer of that democratic journey and, at different stages, worked in cooperation and common purpose with other democratic, left and progressive forces.

Its own political journey also included periods of cooperation with the monarchy, from the establishment of the democratic order to work within the constitutional framework. That accommodation ultimately ended when the monarchy reasserted direct political authority in the early 2000s. Other political forces, through struggle, contestation, adaptation and negotiation, also came to embrace the liberal democratic order and became part of Nepal’s parliamentary experience. The inheritance is therefore larger than any one organization. It includes the aspirations, institutions and practices that helped create a more participatory Nepal and gave successive generations greater room to shape the country’s future.

It is natural, on such an occasion, to look back with pride at what has been accomplished. But it may be more important to ask what kind of country Nepal has become, what remains unfinished, and what the next phase requires. The political and social world in which earlier struggles were fought is no longer the world of today. Nepal is more open, connected, mobile and socially diverse, while expectations have expanded alongside education, technology, migration, communication and economic opportunity. A democratic inheritance cannot remain meaningful simply because of what it achieved in its own time; its continuing value depends on whether it can carry forward the principles and purposes that gave it meaning while speaking to the country that has emerged from that history.

The reversal of established political parties, including the Nepali Congress, in the 2026 election has given these questions particular urgency. It pointed to more than a change in parliamentary arithmetic; it also revealed changing public expectations and a changing relationship between citizens and established political traditions. Against this changing landscape, the party’s 15th general convention is taking place amid an unresolved dispute over organizational legitimacy and questions about its leadership. These immediate questions matter, but they also bring into focus the larger challenge of how a political tradition can renew its relevance in a country that has changed so much.

A younger and more outward-looking population increasingly judges politics not only by historical achievement or ideological commitment, but also by the quality of government, the opportunities available to people and the ability of public institutions to respond to everyday problems. Nepal’s central task has moved beyond creating a political order capable of representing its citizens. It is now to make that order capable of delivering deeper economic transformation, competent government and resilient prosperity. The sections below take up what that requires.

From political change to economic renewal

Nepal’s political transformation created the institutional space within which wider social and economic change could take place. Over the decades, the country has seen the expansion of infrastructure, education, health services, communications, public institutions and markets. The state has acquired a much greater presence across the country, and citizens have gained access to opportunities and forms of communication that were largely unavailable to earlier generations. Yet the productive economy has not advanced at the same pace.

Nepal has developed an industrial base, but industry has not acquired the depth or breadth to drive higher productivity and structural transformation. Manufacturing has not absorbed labor on the scale experienced in countries that followed a sustained industrial path, nor has it generated the degree of domestic production, technological learning and value addition associated with such a course. Agriculture remains important and is increasingly, though still insufficiently, connected to markets, while services have expanded markedly. The result is an economy in which the social and institutional landscape has moved ahead of the productive base that must ultimately sustain it.

Geography is central to this challenge, as both constraint and asset. Nepal’s position between India and China creates possibilities, but location alone does not produce connectivity or economic integration. Connections toward the north remain constrained by rugged Himalayan terrain and limited infrastructure, making the movement of people, goods and investment more difficult and costly.

The value of Nepal’s position will depend on whether infrastructure, institutions and productive capabilities can turn proximity into practical economic opportunity. At the same time, the country’s geography provides some of its greatest economic assets. Rivers and elevation create substantial hydropower potential; mountains, biodiversity and cultural landscapes underpin tourism; and ecological diversity supports distinctive forms of agriculture and local economic activity. Their economic value, however, depends on the infrastructure, skills, investment and markets needed to make sustained and productive use of them.

The future will depend less on identifying a single new engine of growth than on creating conditions in which several sources of productive potential can reinforce one another. Hydropower must connect with industry and markets, tourism with infrastructure and local enterprise, agriculture with technology, finance, storage and processing, and digital connectivity with skills and investment. Regional integration, in turn, depends on reliable physical and institutional networks that allow Nepali producers and businesses to participate effectively. Services also offer scope: information and communication, finance, education, health and other knowledge-based activities. In every sector the task is to turn possibility into productive activity, employment, domestic value addition and stronger linkages.

Progress cannot be judged by aggregate growth alone. What matters is whether the economy creates productive employment, raises productivity, encourages investment and innovation, expands domestic value addition and allows more people to participate in a dynamic economy. Nepal’s difficulty is less a shortage of resources than a shortage of the enterprise, infrastructure, skills and institutions needed to connect them.

A Changing Society and New Expectations

Migration has become one of the clearest expressions of Nepal’s changing economic and social structure. Internal migration has altered the demographic geography of the country, while overseas migration has become deeply embedded in household livelihoods and the wider economy. Remittances have provided an important cushion for families and communities and supported consumption, education, housing and other forms of investment.

At the same time, the scale of outward migration reflects the limited capacity of the domestic economy to provide sufficient productive employment. The longer-term question is not whether migration should be regarded as a problem or a solution. It has become part of Nepal’s economic life. The more useful aim is to connect the skills, experience, networks and resources acquired through migration more closely with productive activity at home. A country cannot indefinitely rely on the export of its labor while importing a large share of what its people consume. Mobility should become a source of capability, not a substitute for opportunity at home.

Nepal is also becoming more urban, mobile and educated, and younger people are increasingly shaped by exposure to opportunities and standards beyond the country. This can become a source of dynamism if education, skills, health, employment and enterprise develop sufficiently to make productive use of human capability. But a demographic dividend is not automatic.

Technology is opening another set of possibilities. Digital connectivity can help overcome some of the disadvantages imposed by geography, widen access to markets and services, facilitate new forms of enterprise and employment, and improve public-service delivery. But technology cannot overcome structural limitations by itself. Its benefits depend on the wider economic and institutional capacity to put it to effective use.

Climate change adds a further dimension. Nepal’s contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions is negligible, while its exposure to climate-related risks is substantial. Climate pressures can affect agriculture and livelihoods, water availability, hydropower, roads and other infrastructure, tourism, settlements and ecosystems. Climate resilience cannot be treated as an environmental concern separate from development. It has to be incorporated into the planning and management of the sectors on which livelihoods and prosperity depend.

This also gives Nepal a distinctive international position. Its negligible contribution to global emissions, combined with serious vulnerability, provides grounds for a stronger voice on climate justice, adaptation, resilience and the concerns of mountain and Himalayan regions. That voice will carry greater weight when accompanied by stronger domestic resilience and the capacity to protect people and productive assets from growing risks.

From political settlement to effective government

These changes bear directly on the state. Citizens look for responsive institutions, good public services, transparency and accountability. Political legitimacy is experienced not only through participation and representation but through the everyday performance of government. The quality of public administration increasingly affects how citizens experience the state itself. Nepal’s political journey has produced a substantial constitutional and institutional settlement.

The transition to a federal democratic republic, a more inclusive constitutional framework, wider representation and devolution of authority have significantly altered how the state is organized and how citizens participate in public life. For the present, the challenge is less further restructuring than making these arrangements work with greater coherence, competence and responsiveness. Debates over federal arrangements and the electoral system will continue, and some adjustment may prove necessary, but citizens now judge the settlement chiefly by how well it performs.

Federalism is an important part of this new architecture. It has brought government closer to citizens and created more room for locally grounded development. Yet weak coordination among levels of government and uneven administrative, technical and fiscal resources have constrained its promise. Local governments hold real potential, but proximity alone does not guarantee good government. Strengthening professional administration, clarifying responsibilities and improving coordination will be central to the years ahead. The same is true beyond domestic administration.

Economic development, infrastructure, migration, urbanisation, technology and climate resilience increasingly require coordination across jurisdictions, while Nepal’s relations with India and China, its place in a changing regional economy, and its growing engagement with global markets and climate diplomacy require coherent and sustained national policy. Nepal needs a state capable of delivering at home while also navigating a complex regional and international environment in pursuit of long-term national interests.

The measure of the present constitutional order will increasingly be found in implementation: the quality of public services, the ability of governments at different levels to work together, the competence of public institutions, and the capacity to turn Nepal’s possibilities into tangible improvements in people’s lives.

Renewal and continuity

The moment matters beyond this general convention. Nepal’s political arrangements have evolved alongside a society whose expectations of politics and government have shifted markedly. Yet the productive and institutional weaknesses described above remain, and they cannot be overcome by political change alone. Democratic institutions must continue to respond to the society they have helped create and to the expectations that have grown around them.

For the Nepali Congress, the moment is significant not simply because of the organisational questions immediately before it, but because it brings into focus a larger question about the future of a political tradition that has played such a consequential role in Nepal’s history. The experience, democratic commitments and sense of public purpose accumulated over eight decades must remain relevant to a society that has itself changed profoundly. The task is thoughtful renewal: understanding what is worth preserving, what needs to change and what the future demands.

That renewal calls for a closer relationship between political achievement and institutional performance. Representation remains fundamental, but it must be accompanied by capable government and meaningful opportunity. Together, these are the larger test facing Nepal’s political order: whether the gains of the past can be converted into a more capable state and wider prosperity. Political traditions still matter here. They carry memories of struggle, institutional experience and public trust accumulated over time.

A tradition that has served the nation well has much worth preserving, but preservation cannot mean standing still. History can provide a foundation; it cannot guarantee continued relevance or public confidence. Those have to be earned again by understanding the country as it is becoming and responding to the aspirations of those who will shape its future. That requires the courage to ask what once made a political tradition meaningful to people and useful to the nation, and to give those qualities new expression in changed circumstances. Democratic conviction, a connection with ordinary citizens, a sense of public service and commitment to a larger national purpose are not relics of an earlier era. Their value lies precisely in how they are carried forward by each new generation.

There is nothing wrong with looking back with affection. Political journeys are made not only through institutions and ideas, but through friendships, sacrifices, shared struggles and memories that remain long after particular moments have passed. For someone like me who has been part of such a journey, attachment is inevitably personal. It is a source of gratitude, and quiet pride, to have shared, however modestly, in a cause larger than any individual: the advancement of democracy and the building of the nation.

That association carries a responsibility to look at the present with candor, including the disagreements and strains that accompany a period of transition, and to look to the future with faith. To care for a political tradition is not to shield it from difficult truths or from the need to change; it is to want it to retain its connection with people, its public purpose and its capacity to serve the country as it is becoming. Precisely because that inheritance matters, it deserves neither uncritical celebration nor easy dismissal, but an honest reckoning with what should be preserved, what must change and what may have been lost along the way.

Every political generation eventually makes room for another. But democratic renewal need not mean a rupture between them. New leadership will necessarily see Nepal through somewhat different eyes, speak more directly to people whose experiences differ from those of their predecessors, and bring expectations that earlier leaders could not have fully anticipated. But successors also inherit a debt: to the pioneers who carried the cause of liberty; to those who devoted themselves to the dignity and well-being of ordinary people; to the builders of modern Nepal; to those who carried that responsibility forward; and to the martyrs who gave their lives for it.

Their sacrifices gave meaning to a political tradition whose deepest inheritance is not simply memory, but the democratic and national purpose entrusted to them. The accumulated wisdom of a long political experience can offer guidance, but those who come next must have the freedom to bring their own language, priorities and imagination to the democratic enterprise. Continuity gives renewal a foundation; renewal gives continuity a future.

A new chapter does not erase the pages that came before it. It carries their lessons forward while accepting that the story must be written in circumstances that have changed. The hope, then, should not be for a return to an earlier political moment or for change for its own sake, but for a future that preserves what was strongest in the democratic traditions that helped shape modern Nepal, learns honestly from what has not worked, and gives each new generation the freedom to bring its own experience and imagination to that inheritance.

When the party looks back from its centenary, it should be able to do so with gratitude for the journey, honesty about what remains unfinished, affection for what was built, and confidence in those who have carried and will carry the work forward. The present period of disagreement should ultimately matter less as an organisational dispute than as a test of whether the Congress can emerge with a stronger sense of purpose, a deeper connection with the people and a greater capacity to meet the demands of a changing Nepal. The ultimate measure will be whether its deepest democratic and national purpose can continue to command the trust of the people it sought to serve, and whether that inheritance can be made meaningful to the Nepal of its time.

May the next chapter carry that inheritance into the Nepal of today, renewing its democratic purpose for a new generation. May those entrusted with it bring fresh eyes, fresh energy and a renewed sense of purpose, while drawing wisdom from the experience that made their work possible. And may that continuing journey contribute to the larger unfinished task before us all: building a more prosperous, inclusive, capable and resilient Nepal.

title: Death toll rises to 15 after avalanche at Mount Himlung base camp in Nepal - news.cgtn.com
description: Death toll rises to 15 after avalanche at Mount Himlung base camp in Nepal  news.cgtn.com
publisher.title: news.cgtn.com
full_article:
Search teams recovered eight more bodies from an avalanche site at the base camp of Mount Himlung in Nepal's Manang district on Thursday, bringing the death toll to 15, an official said.

Two of the recovered bodies were airlifted to the district hospital in Chame, while six were transported to Phu village in the district.

"Of the 16 people missing in the disaster, 15 bodies have been recovered as of Thursday. Although all the belongings of the last missing person have been found, he is yet to be traced," said Krishna Prasad Paudel, assistant chief district officer.

The 16 people, including mountain guides and kitchen staff from two expedition companies, were at the base camp of the 7,126-meter peak to prepare camps and fix ropes when the avalanche struck early Sunday morning.

Paudel said the search for the last missing person would continue on Friday.

title: Dispute over social democracy intensifies in Nepali Congress — Kathmandu Post - UA.NEWS
description: Dispute over social democracy intensifies in Nepali Congress — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, an internal party dispute over its ideological course has intensified ahead of the 15th general convention of the Nepali Congress. Part of the leadership proposes updating the traditional doctrine of democratic socialism of the party’s founder, Bishweshwar Prasad Koirala, and incorporating the concept of social democracy into it. Supporters of former president Sher Bahadur Deuba oppose this approach. This was reported by Kathmandu Post.

Dispute after the special convention

The discussion intensified after the party’s special general convention in January, at which Gagan Thapa became president of the Nepali Congress. The document adopted then introduced the concept of social democracy and provided for updating the party’s principles, ideas and policies in line with public demands.

Deuba’s faction believes that the new leadership is moving away from the fundamental socialist course and jeopardizing the party’s historical identity. Its representatives also seek to hold a parallel general convention. Thapa’s supporters deny abandoning Koirala’s legacy, stressing that the aim is to clarify and modernize socialist ideas in accordance with contemporary political, economic and social conditions.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Economy and the younger generation

Party General Secretary Pradip Paudel stated that socialism remains the ideal of the Nepali Congress, but its content must evolve with the times. He also acknowledged that the party needs to define its economic policy more clearly. Congress leader Shyam Ghimire called for an emphasis on an open economy, the private sector and Nepal’s integration into the global economy, while leaving the state with the role of a regulator that ensures equal opportunities and fair distribution of resources.

Former party spokesperson Prakash Sharan Mahat, who belongs to Deuba’s faction, said in turn that a move toward social democracy could weaken the traditional identity of the Nepali Congress. In his view, the party should adhere to a model in which production is provided by the private sector and the state guarantees the fair distribution of resources.

An additional factor in the debate was the rise of the Rastriya Swatantra Party, which became the largest party in the House of Representatives after winning the March election and officially adopted social democracy as its ideology in June. Following the introduction of quotas for representatives under the age of 35, young leaders of the Nepali Congress are also seeking ideological renewal. One young delegate, Umanga Lohani, called on candidates for leadership positions to focus on good governance, a corruption-free society and youth issues.

title: Opinion | Nepal must turn satellite observations into early warnings - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | Nepal must turn satellite observations into early warnings  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The catastrophe that swept through the Lhende Khola–Bhotekoshi–Trishuli corridor on August 26, 2026, exposed not only the growing instability of a warming Himalaya, but also a dangerous gap between what modern science can observe and what our institutions are prepared to do with that knowledge. Closing that gap must become a national priority for Nepal and a regional priority across the Hindu-Kush Himalaya.

The Himalayas are exceptionally difficult to monitor. Nepal cannot place technicians and instruments on every glacier, unstable slope or high-altitude river. Many locations remain inaccessible for months. Ground instruments are costly to install and maintain, and floods or landslides can destroy the very gauges designed to detect them. The challenge is also transboundary: hazards may originate beyond Nepal’s borders while threatening communities, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities and trade routes inside the country.

For terrain this vast, satellite remote sensing is indispensable. But satellites alone do not save lives. A scientific signal becomes useful only when someone is continuously looking for it, qualified experts can interpret it, authorities know what action to take and exposed communities receive a warning they understand and trust.

In response to the Rasuwa tragedy, a webinar titled “The Himalayan Tsunami: Science, Technology and Innovation for a Safer Nepal” was held on September 18, 2026. The event brought together Nepali and international experts in remote sensing, mountain science, Earth observation, disaster risk reduction, technology and public communication. The discussion was encouraging. It showed that considerable expertise already exists among scientists in Nepal, the Nepali diaspora, international universities and institutions such as ICIMOD.

During the webinar, Virginia Tech geophysicist Professor Manoochehr Shirzaei reported that satellite radar images suggested part of the glacier-rock system had been moving and accelerating in the weeks before its collapse. His preliminary analysis of Sentinel-1 radar data taken from January 8 to August 18 (until a week before the incident) detected movement of roughly 10 millimetres per month near the apparent failure zone. He also cautioned that the precise sequence of events remained uncertain and that such movement, considered in isolation, would not necessarily predict an imminent catastrophe.

Another presenter, Robert Rohde, chief scientist at Berkeley Earth, reported that his team had analysed meteorological conditions surrounding the August 26 collapse and subsequent flash floods in Nepal and Tibet. The analysis indicated exceptional heat at the high-altitude site immediately before the disaster—conditions that may have contributed to the rock-and-ice avalanche.

Average temperatures at the collapse site, located at an altitude of approximately 5,200 metres, reached roughly 5 degrees Celsius between August 21 and 26. This level of heat was unprecedented for that specific time of year; temperatures during this six-day window had never exceeded 4.0 degrees Celsius in more than 55 years of historical records.

This distinction is important. This research does not prove that the August 26 disaster could have been predicted with certainty. It does, however, raise an urgent question: If scientists can detect potentially significant deformation after an event, why is there no operational system routinely monitoring for similar changes before disaster strikes?

Early-warning systems require continuous data acquisition, automated analysis, trained staff working under clear protocols, predefined alert thresholds, rapid human verification and an institution authorised to act.

To achieve this, Nepal needs a multi-scale approach. The country has capable scientists and agencies, but the chain connecting observation, interpretation and public warning remains fragmented. Furthermore, Nepal alone may not be able to achieve this goal. It should connect its national warning system with existing international Earth-observation research and operational monitoring networks.

An effective Earth observation system would integrate radar, optical, thermal, hyperspectral and lidar observations. Synthetic aperture radar can observe through clouds and darkness and measure subtle ground deformation. Optical imagery can reveal changes in glaciers, lakes, river channels and slopes. Thermal data can help identify unusual melt or freeze-thaw conditions. Hyperspectral imagery can distinguish snow, ice, water, vegetation and surface materials in greater detail. Periodic LiDAR surveys can produce precise terrain models and measure changes in unstable valleys. Geostationary satellites provide frequent observations of weather systems, while sun-synchronous satellites provide more detailed repeat coverage.

“Fortunately, much of the necessary satellite data is freely available,” said Barbara Ryan, former Executive Director of the Group on Earth Observations (GEO), during the webinar.

Artificial intelligence (AI) can compare observations from multiple sensors, detect acceleration or unusual change, and rank locations for expert review. It can reduce the impossible task of manually examining thousands of images to the manageable task of investigating a smaller number of anomalies. AI should be used to prioritise anomalies for expert review—not to issue public warnings without human verification.

During the webinar, engineer Abinash Silwal presented preliminary results from reconstructing the disaster using Earth observation data and advanced analytical methods. These findings could help scientists better understand the event and inform future monitoring efforts.

Basanta Shrestha, former Director of Strategic Cooperation and head of the MENRIS program at ICIMOD, noted that “ICIMOD has been using satellite data to monitor glaciers for 30 years, but a new approach is now needed.”

The Nepal government should consolidate, update and operationalise existing inventories of glaciers, unstable rock-ice slopes, moraine-dammed lakes and landslide-prone valleys. High-risk locations should be analysed whenever new radar or optical data become available, daily where suitable imagery exists and as frequently as technically possible elsewhere. Commercial imagery should be purchased selectively when free satellite data reveal concerning changes. Additionally, satellite monitoring must be connected to ground truthing. Automatic weather stations, river gauges, seismic and acoustic sensors, cameras, and GNSS instruments should be installed at the highest-risk sites.

Nepal also needs a 24/7 operational warning desk with legally defined responsibilities. An anomaly in satellite data should automatically open a case, trigger expert review, and, when necessary, place downstream authorities on watch. The country must establish formal partnerships with regional and international scientific institutions to share near-real-time satellite, meteorological, hydrological and seismic information.

Remote sensing cannot prevent glaciers from collapsing or mountains from moving. Nor can it guarantee that every disaster will be predicted. But it can reveal changes in places human observers cannot reach, provide precious time for investigation, and guide warnings before a hazard becomes a catastrophe.

description: Nepal introduces federal civil service bill in parliament — Kathmandu Post  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
In Nepal, the government has registered the long-awaited Federal Civil Service Bill in the House of Representatives. The document is intended to consolidate civil service provisions and create a legal basis for administrative federalism, Kathmandu Post reports.

The bill was registered on Thursday, one day before the scheduled end of the current session of the federal parliament. Under House of Representatives rules, a document can be presented for consideration at least seven days after registration, so debates may begin no earlier than the winter session.

Transitional pension rules

The provisions on retirement age sparked the most controversy. The bill proposes raising the mandatory retirement age for civil servants from 58 to 60. At the same time, a one-time transitional rule provides for the retirement of employees who will be 55 when the law comes into force or who will have 30 years of service.

The final version of the bill includes protection of pension payments for civil servants affected by early retirement. According to officials, employees who leave service before turning 58 will not lose benefits to which they would have been entitled under the current system. Those with 30 years of service who have not yet reached age 58 may have up to seven additional years counted toward their pension calculation, depending on their age.

According to the Department of National Personnel Records, if the 55-30 provision is adopted, 39 of the 53 incumbent secretaries — more than 73% — will have to retire. Former chief secretary Leelamani Paudyal warned that the simultaneous departure of a large number of experienced officials could create problems for preserving institutional memory, decision-making and leadership.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Appointments and service in provinces

The document also reduces the terms in office for top officials: from three to two years for the chief secretary and from five to three years for secretaries. A separate provision allows the government to appoint outside specialists for a fixed term to specialized executive or expert positions if the civil service system lacks the necessary personnel. Before such an appointment, the government must consult the Public Service Commission.

The bill provides for provincial civil services up to the 12th level. Provincial chief secretaries will remain employees of the federal civil service, seconded by the federal government from among 13th-level officials. Secretaries of provincial ministries will belong to the 12th level of the provincial service, and their working conditions will be determined by provincial legislation.

Quotas and post-service restrictions

The share of positions reserved for inclusive groups in open competition is proposed to increase from 45% to 49%. Half of this quota is planned to be allocated to women. The quota system is to be reviewed every 10 years, and reservation benefits may be used only once for non-gazetted category posts and once for gazetted category posts.

In addition, the bill retains a two-year restriction period for senior officials after dismissal or retirement. Former special-class and first-class officials will not be able to hold constitutional, diplomatic or other state positions for two years. The document also contains provisions on interprovincial transfers, leadership assessments, the absence of trade unions in the civil service, and menstrual leave.

publisher.title: The Straits Times
full_article:
NUWAKOT, Nepal – Clutching a photograph of his missing son, Rajesh Ram is pinning his hopes on DNA testing – like thousands of others desperately seeking relatives swept away by Nepal’s catastrophic Himalayan floods.

“I searched for him everywhere, but I could not find his body,” 53-year-old Ram told AFP, still waiting for answers about his son Suroj Kumar, a garage mechanic in Betrawati, which was swamped by the floods.

Nepal was overwhelmed by the sheer scale of destruction from the tsunami-like wall of freezing water and debris triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on the Nepal-China border on Aug 26.

The scale of the identification task is immense.

With thousands of DNA profiles to process , fragmented remains and limited technical capacity and manpower, experts warn matching bodies to families could take weeks.

Nepali disaster authorities have recovered 1,454 bodies – but around a third of those are only partial remains.

Just 112 bodies have been identified and returned to their families. A further 5,285 people are missing in Nepal, including hundreds of foreigners.

In China, the toll is 43 dead and 519 missing, according to state media – taking the combined toll to nearly 1,500 dead and 5,800 missing.

At Nepal’s two forensic laboratories, both in Kathmandu, experts are working to profile samples and build a database on a scale they have never handled before.

“In a year we would analyse 1,000-1,500 samples, often in case of paternity or crime scenes,” said Mukul Pradhan, chief scientific officer at the National Forensic Science Laboratory. “We are now processing thousands of samples.”

‘Pain’

A total of 3,685 forensic samples are undergoing DNA testing, including more than 1,300 collected from recovered bodies.

Blood samples are easier to profile, but those taken from teeth or bones can take several days to process.

Nepal has buried more than 1,200 bodies , carefully numbering and tagging them so they can be retrieved if a DNA match is found.

“A large number of people are missing, and the bodies that have been found they are difficult to identify,” said Nepali police spokesman Abi Narayan Kafle. “We understand the pain people are in, and our teams are working diligently.”

Some bodies were carried far downstream by the floodwaters, further complicating the task, said Nirajan Thapa, Chief of Biology section at the National Forensic Science Laboratory.

“In an earthquake or an accident, people are recovered in a specific area, so we work in a closed scenario – the body’s DNA has to be compared to a limited number of samples,” Thapa said. “But that scale has now become very large.”

DNA alone cannot identify a body without a reference sample from a relative.

“Just by extracting a DNA profile is not enough to identify someone,” Thapa said. “We have to extract a DNA profile from their relatives and then compare”.

That means authorities must process samples from both unidentified remains and thousands of relatives before they can establish matches.

Several countries have sent in support teams, including neighbouring India and China, as well as South Korea. Fingerprint experts from the United States and Singapore are also assisting.

Thapa said that with that help, matching could begin within a few weeks.

But until the results come, the families behind those samples face a painful limbo. Some families have held symbolic cremation funerals for the missing.

Ram wonders if he will ever get any answers. “I am waiting if I can find any remains of my son,” he said. AFP

title: When is a dead person really dead? - Nepali Times
description: When is a dead person really dead?  Nepali Times

full_article:
Total death toll of the Trishuli Valley flood is likely to surpass 7,000. But only 1,453 bodies have been recovered with less than 10% of them identified.

This disproportionate figure in recovery and identification more than a month after the 26 August catastrophe is yet another measure of the enormity of this disaster.

For families of the missing this has been the most grueling – and sometimes gruesome – task. They have had to pore through graphic photographs of hundreds of corpses at hospital morgues, provide DNA samples and wait for news. And then wait some more.

This lack of closure has prolonged the trauma of loss for many families in Nepal and abroad. Forensic experts say that given Nepal’s resources, and despite outside help, it may take months to identify remains in morgues and temporary mass burial sites deep in the forests of Chitwan, Gokarna, Pokhara and Nawalparasi.

“We have to speed it up as much as we can but there are issues of human resources and technical expertise. What the government could have done was set up a Disaster Victim Identification Team to better manage the whole thing,” adds forensic expert Harihar Wasti who worked to exhume bodies during the Maoist conflict.

He adds: “It will take another six months or even a year for all the bodies and body parts to be identified. In the meantime, we have to make sure our social protection mechanisms for the survivors are in place and working.”

Most families have given up hope of ever finding the remains of their loved ones and held symbolic funerals. Others have questioned the delay in DNA identification being done in just two government facilities: the Central Forensic Science Laboratory and the National Forensic Science Laboratory. India, China, Japan, South Korea, Japan, Singapore, Australia and the United States whose nationals are among the 650 people from 38 countries still missing, have also sent forensic experts and equipment.

Till this week, only 112 bodies had been identified and handed over to relatives. Family members have submitted 2,060 DNA samples, and 1,329 tissue samples have been collected from recovered bodies. The labs are racing against time to identify the remaining 1,341 recovered bodies.

“The number of bodies or parts recovered is not a large processing number, but there are several factors that might be contributing to the backlog,” explains Dibesh Karmacharya of the Centre for Molecular Dynamics Nepal. “First, how many bodies or parts were recovered, from where and in what condition. Next, is the DNA database with the samples of next of kin.

Karmacharya is surprised that only 10% of the recovered bodies have been identified so far despite international support: “It is quite low. Private facilities like ours have the technical know-how, and capacity to help and we cannot understand why the government is seeking more expensive and time-consuming international partners when there is domestic expertise readily available.”

Other experts say that fingerprint examination of bodies recovered after the first few days and matched with official documents could have sped up ID. Extracting DNA profiles from decomposed bodies or fragmented remains require complex processing of bone and teeth, taking significantly longer than standard blood or soft-tissue extraction.

There are legal ramifications to the delay. Lack of a death certificate means family members could be denied relief, compensation and insurance. This may especially affect children who lost both parents in the flood but cannot be declared orphaned and get access limited state benefits. Their parents are technically ‘missing’, not dead.

Section 40 of Nepal’s National Civil Code 2017 stipulates that under ‘normal circumstances’ a person cannot be declared dead until they have been missing for 12 years. But the law in its current form already has a provision allowing for judicial declaration of death without a wait period in times of disasters. Which is why the delay in issuing death certificates is so puzzling.

“Under Section 40(4) of the Civil Code, if a person disappears in a natural disaster, a relative can immediately file for a Judicial Declaration of Death at the district court,” explains advocate Indu Tuladhar. “We already have necessary legal provisions to address the current crisis. What we should focus on is streamlining the process for families, maybe by adding more officials, and deploying the apex court in Rasuwa, Dhading and Nuwakot.”

She adds: “The bigger legal issue could be issuing citizenships to children whose parents and relatives have all perished. If we don’t document them all now, a few years down the line when we have all forgotten this disaster, the children will face a bigger legal battle.”

The Home Ministry has drafted an amendment to the statute to streamline death registration and relief for relatives who have lost kin in disasters. For the relatives of the missing and those waiting for identification of bodies, that cannot come soon enough.
